title: We face paying £9,000 tax even though our second home is in a war zone
description: Image caption, Kateryna and Mattias have had to postpone their plans to buy a new homeByMunenyasha SigaukeBBC Scotland NewsA Ukrainian woman who fled
body: Image caption, Kateryna and Mattias have had to postpone their plans to buy a new homeByMunenyasha SigaukeBBC Scotland NewsA Ukrainian woman who fled to Scotland after Russia invaded her homeland has been told she could face a £9,000 property tax charge because she still owns a flat in Kyiv. Kateryna Stepanovych, 38, discovered the potential charge when she tried to buy a house in North Ayrshire with her Scottish partner Mattias Lindgren. The couple were told the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS) charge would apply because she already owned a property overseas. Kateryna bought the small flat in 2018, before Russia's invasion. She fled the war zone in 2023, leaving the property behind. Image source, Kateryna StepanovychImage caption, Kateryna says the 10-storey building in Kyiv where she has an apartment was hit by shrapnel in an attack in 2023The conflict has seen shrapnel strike the front of her 10-storey apartment building, damaging its exterior and a neighbouring property. Her own flat remained undamaged. "The fact that the property is still there is a miracle," Mattias said. The couple, who currently live in Stromness in Orkney, only became aware of the £9,000 charge when they put down an offer on the property they were planning to buy and Mattias looked through the paperwork from their solicitor. Unable to afford the additional cost, they had to withdraw their offer. Mattias said: "Why should we be punished with this tax for a property that's in a war zone?" Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kyiv has come under regular attack since Russia invaded in 2022Under Revenue Scotland's rules, the Additional Dwelling Supplement Charge can see house buyers facing an additional 8% charge if they already own another property, including overseas.It was introduced by the Scottish government primarily to target people who are buying second or buy-to-let homes and is paid in addition to Land and Buildings Transaction Tax. The couple got in touch with Orkney MSP Liam McArthur in the summer after being told by their solicitors there was nothing they could do about the charge.McArthur then contacted Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth, who responded with a letter which stated that there are "no provisions within the legislation that allow either the Scottish government or Revenue Scotland to disapply ADS on a discretionary or case-by-case basis." Image source, Press AssociationImage caption, The couple's case was raised in the Scottish Parliament by Liam McArthurLib Dem MSP McArthur raised the couple's case in the Scottish Parliament on Tuesday, when he asked First Minister John Swinney whether he "agrees with me that this is surely not the intended purpose of the tax?" Swinney said he would ask Revenue Scotland to investigate the case, adding that he could understand why the rules had created the situation the couple were facing. Kateryna and Mattias had hoped to relocate this year, but are now considering renting while postponing their plans to buy. "It's been quite hard because we've had to rethink how we're approaching buying a property," Mattias said. Kateryna, who works in a factory, has found dealing with the issue particularly challenging because English is not her first language. "For me, it's difficult," she said, adding there was little else she could do beyond providing documents from Ukraine.The couple said they are now "biding our time" while exploring their options.

schema.headline: We face paying £9,000 tax even though our second home is in a war zone

title: England 45-22 Australia: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso burns bright in win
description: "Plastic energy."That's what Bongi Mbonambi described it as.After scraping past Steve Borthwick's side in the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final, the Sou
body: "Plastic energy."That's what Bongi Mbonambi described it as.After scraping past Steve Borthwick's side in the 2023 Rugby World Cup semi-final, the South Africa hooker was scathing of England's back-slapping and celebrating of in-game wins.By then, it had already become something of a meme. Back row Ben Earl pumping his fist to celebrate Ireland's crooked line-out throw in a pre-tournament warm-up was a particular source of online mockery.But, while it isn't the diesel grunt that can win matches on its own, "plastic energy" is still something.It is the body language that shows mindset and intent, that a team's pilot light is on and burning bright.England had it under Borthwick at the Stade de France three years ago, coming agonisingly close to derailing the Springboks. And they had it in spades in Sunday's 45-22 win against the Wallabies.Earl, inevitably, was one outlet, loudly celebrating a third-minute scrum success.But there were plenty more examples throughout the match. Jamie George bellowing into the stands after the opening score; captain Maro Itoje being surrounded with congratulations after an early charge-down; Henry Slade being embraced after a lung-busting late try-saving tackle on Max Jorgensen.Borthwick needed it all.A report in the Times newspaper earlier in the week had said that a rift between the players and their coach opened in Argentina in July, at the end of the summer's campaign.England's senior players denied it. Nothing more to see, they said, than the transparent honesty of a team where input is valued and improvement is the lodestar.But, they also promised proof on the pitch against Australia. It was a risky gambit.Another misfiring, disjointed, underpowered performance – like that in their most-recent visit to Twickenham, February's 42-21 defeat by Ireland  - would dial up the pressure on Borthwick another notch.Instead, his fired-up players turned up.They did so in the obvious ways. There was gainline physicality, breakdown bravery and crunching physicality.Ben Curry leaping out of the line to land a big hit on fly-half Declan Meredith was satisfyingly old school.But there was more than that. There was a different sort of bravery – the one that dares to chance the arm, throw a final pass and back ability, rather than take a safe option.Full-back George Furbank summed it up. Playing his first Test in nearly two years, his ball-playing smarts were deliciously demonstrated in Jack van Poortvliet's try, hitting a line, flashing a dummy and smuggling an offload to cut the Wallabies to ribbons.Henry Slade and Seb Atkinson pulled strings expertly as well.Immanuel Feyi-Waboso showed the sort of Test match mojo that England must protect at all costs.The Exeter wing, who, like Furbank, has endured a rotten injury run, was electric in the first half.Every time the 23-year-old touched the ball, expectation crackled around the stands. And it was mostly met.In 40 minutes of rugby, Feyi-Waboso made 113m from eight carries, beating seven defenders.All those figures were unmatched by any other England player despite the fact that Feyi-Waboso came off at the break and only played 32 minutes uninjured.The wing's ankle was caught under prop Angus Bell's considerable heft and was cossetted in a protective boot as he watched the remainder of the match from the sidelines.After Feyi-Waboso's absence from the entirety of England's Six Nations campaign, the decision not to remove him immediately and minimise the damage may be one they regret when the prognosis lands.England looked to his pace, power and unpredictability as much as they could, feeding him on a dart off the blindside wing from one promising line-out position.They may be missing it next week against Japan. And potentially beyond.Henry Pollock, with a shock of freshly-peroxided hair, came on and inevitably stole the spotlight, with two tries in a cameo on the wing.But, on the wing, Pollock is a stop-gap, while Feyi-Waboso is the star.His fitness, along with that of Seb Atkinson, will be chief of Borthwick's concerns.A cleaned-up disciplinary display – with seven penalties conceded and only the second time this year they have managed to avoid being shown a card – and breakdown that was quick and clean were major plus points.The bench maintained their dominance with an all-Lions front row of Ellis Genge, Luke Cowan-Dickie and Will Stuart trotting on to turn the screw was a welcome sight."I am really proud," Borthwick told BBC Sport. "These players are a wonderful group. We have had some bumps in the road. We have this age bubble where we have so many players 25 and under who are developing quickly into great Test match players, and we have an older group who are helping to guide them."It is an interesting balance and they are working so well together. They are a pleasure to work with."There are big caveats.Australia were desperately poor. Their players are in the midst of a pay dispute with Rugby Australia, an unwelcome distraction that has gone under the radar given the focus on Borthwick.New Zealand, rejuvenated under new coach Dave Rennie, will offer a far more formidable stress test in a fortnight.But as the team's energy spread to the stands, with the vast majority of the 81,334 won over by the display, Sunday was a victory for England to savour at the end of a difficult week.

schema.headline: England 45-22 Australia: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso burns bright in win

title: Paris Masters: Carlos Alcaraz takes revenge on Ben Shelton to win title for first time
description: Just 60 days after his comeback tournament was ended in a late-night New York blockbuster against Ben Shelton, Carlos Alcaraz took his revenge.In doin
body: Just 60 days after his comeback tournament was ended in a late-night New York blockbuster against Ben Shelton, Carlos Alcaraz took his revenge.In doing so, the Spaniard offered the latest indication that his ascension back to the top of the men's game is nearing completion.Alcaraz exceeded expectations when, on his return from four months out with a wrist injury, he reached the US Open quarter-finals in September before going out in an astonishing five-set epic against rising American star Shelton.In the two months since, Alcaraz has won three titles and lost once in 17 matches.Victory over world number four Shelton on Sunday sealed the 23-year-old's first triumph at the prestigious Paris Masters 1000 tournament. It also confirmed a fully-fit Alcaraz, who has now won seven of the nine ATP Masters 1000 events, will once again be ready to compete for the sport's major prizes in 2027.Following his 7-6 (7-5) 7-5 triumph, Alcaraz said: "It's something I've been chasing for a long time. I had some of the toughest losses of my career here."Today was one of the toughest challenges we have in tennis right now, facing Ben. Great champion, great player, great person. He is doing better and better every tournament. From here, it is going to be even tougher facing him."I'm just really happy that I finally got it. This tournament is really special."That indomitable spirit was again on display as Alcaraz saved all six break points against him in a tense opening set against Shelton, who himself was fearless after a stellar year in which he has won four titles and reached a first major final.Both players demonstrated admirable poise under pressure, with Shelton also seeing off two break points, but it was Alcaraz who held his nerve to take the first-set tie-break by winning four of the final five points from 4-3 down.Shelton finally capitalised when Alcaraz opened the door in an error-strewn third service game in the second set. But, with the set in his sights as he served for a 5-3 lead, Alcaraz struck back.The Spaniard pointed to his ear in a call for more noise from the crowd after edging a breathless exchange to hold for a 5-4 advantage, his confidence clear as he danced to the music inside the stadium during the change of ends.It was not long before Alcaraz raised his arms in celebration after ending Shelton's resistance on a second match point, embracing his team courtside after closing out the title by winning five of the final six games.It was a ninth ATP Masters 1000 crown overall for Alcaraz, and left Canada and Shanghai as the only titles he requires to emulate Novak Djokovic and Jannik Sinner as just the third man to win all nine tournaments at that level.Great Britain's Henry Patten and doubles partner Harri Heliovaara have secured the year-end world number one ranking for the first time.The Wimbledon champions, who only joined forces in 2024, confirmed they will end a successful 2026 as the top-ranked men's doubles pairing with their run to the semi-finals in Paris, which also sealed their place at the ATP Finals.Patten and Heliovaara reclaimed their Wimbledon title this summer and also triumphed in Adelaide, Doha, Dubai and Madrid.Patten said: "It's an incredible achievement, one that goes to the very top of my list of best achievements as a tennis player. "When I look back on the journey me and Harri have been on together when we started in 2024, I was ranked around number 60 in the world and Harri was around  40."In two years we've worked incredibly hard and to go from where we started to where we are now, on top of the world, is beautiful."Heliovaara said: "One of the crazy dreams comes true again. A few years ago I would have never imagined this could be possible."

schema.headline: Paris Masters: Carlos Alcaraz takes revenge on Ben Shelton to win title for first time

title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
description: Figure caption, Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in EgyptByEmer MoreauAt least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egypti
body: Figure caption, Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in EgyptByEmer MoreauAt least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment. Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Uninjured passengers and bystanders searched derailed carriages for injured peopleThe government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.Image source, Getty ImagesTrains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

schema.headline: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt

title: Two arrested after police officers hurt in brawl outside Glasgow bare-knuckle fighting event
description: Image source, Gregory HoareImage caption, Officers quickly arrived after young men were seen fighting on the Clyde Arc bridgeTwo men have been arreste
body: Image source, Gregory HoareImage caption, Officers quickly arrived after young men were seen fighting on the Clyde Arc bridgeTwo men have been arrested and three police officers injured during a street disturbance outside a bare-knuckle fighting championship in Glasgow. Footage circulating on social media shows a group of men trading punches in the street outside  the Ovo Hydro where the event was held on Saturday evening.More than 20 police vehicles and a police helicopter converged on the area. Three officers were hurt, two of them requiring medical treatment, as they responded to the disorder. Police Scotland said two men, aged 32 and 27, had been arrested and charged with offences including assault, obstructing police and threatening and abusive behaviour. Figure caption, More than 20 police vehicles converged on the area outside Glasgow's Ovo Hydro after violence broke out in nearby streetsThousands of spectators had earlier gathered for the Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship (BKFC) event where Sean Weir from Wishaw defeated Leigh Cohoon from Manchester when the referee stopped the fight in the first round. At about 23:10, police said they received reports of a large disturbance in the Congress Road area outside the venue. Image caption, Police Scotland said three officers were injured, two of them requiring medical treatementCh Insp Paul Daley said: "Several officers were assaulted whilst carrying out their duties during disorder following an event at the Hydro in Glasgow on Saturday night."Violence against officers is disgraceful and will not be tolerated. Being assaulted is not part of the job and it's extremely fortunate they were not seriously injured."The two men who have been charged will be reported to prosecutors. Three other men were arrested and issued with recorded police warnings for threatening and abusive behaviour and breach of the peace. Police said inquiries were continuing and that anyone found responsible "will be brought to justice". They have asked anyone with information about the disturbance to contact them., external

schema.headline: Two arrested after police officers hurt in brawl outside Glasgow bare-knuckle fighting event

title: Why now's not the time to put your feet up before Christmas
description: Doing these things now will help you save money at ChristmasImage source, Getty/ Tanja IvanovaByCost of living correspondentHow soon is too soon when
body: Doing these things now will help you save money at ChristmasImage source, Getty/ Tanja IvanovaByCost of living correspondentHow soon is too soon when it comes to thinking about Christmas and your finances?The answer, of course, is that it is never too soon. Save early and the cost becomes more manageable.The squeeze is harder for some than others, with charity Barnardo's warning that some parents will skip meals so their kids get a Christmas dinner with the trimmings.But, debt advice charity StepChange is offering tips to everyone, to avoid Christmas spending leading to a financially painful new year.What to think about nowThe best way to avoid a difficult January, it says, is to make a realistic plan before the spending begins. Small decisions now can make a big difference later. Its tips include:Budget for Christmas in full. So, that's not just presents, a budget should include the cost of food and drink, travel, parties, presents, postage, decorations and other festive extrasSpread the cost. Don't just rely on your December paypacket. Also, make a shopping list before Black Friday on 27 November - it is only a discount if you were going to buy it anywayBook your train journey now. Advance tickets, if available, are cheaperSet spending limits. Put a cap on the bill for Christmas socialising, and have a quiet conversation with family and friends about how much to spend on presentsStocktake before the big food shop. Check your cupboards, fridge and freezer before you go shopping and plan meals around food you already have. Make a list of what you need and compare prices.Think twice. Can you afford what you are going to buy? Can you afford the repayments if it's bought on credit? And, do you really need it?"Christmas is a time when we want to enjoy ourselves and make things special for the people we care most about," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive of StepChange."But it can also put a lot of pressure on household budgets, and it is key to take steps to get ahead of any January financial blues."Where to go for helpIf you are concerned about Christmas leaving you in debt, then it is best to seek advice well before things become unmanageable. The independent MoneyHelper website has a guide to finding free debt advice near you, external.There are also tools to work out if you are receiving all the benefits and grants you are entitled to, and tips on how to draw up a budget.And it is really important to watch out for scams at this time of year. Fraudsters will take any opportunity to catch you out, especially when you are under pressure financially.

schema.headline: Why now's not the time to put your feet up before Christmas

title: Maya Jama steps down as host of reality TV show Love Island
description: Presenter Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of reality TV show Love Island after three years.The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram
body: Presenter Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of reality TV show Love Island after three years.The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram alongside a highlights reel of her on the programme that it was "time to throw myself into something new"."While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I'll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever," the TV and radio presenter said.Jama's announcement comes hot on the heels of an appearance as a contestant on Celebrity Traitors that won her praise and speculation in the Times, external that she could "get £1m per deal" thanks to her success.Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an "unforgettable time" on the programme."I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I've loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.But she added: "I've always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then."Jama landed her biggest presenting role to date as the host of the reality TV show in 2023, taking over from Laura Whitmore.The programme couples contestants together who then complete a range of tasks and keep swapping in the hope of meeting the love of their life.An ITV spokesperson said: "Maya has been a fantastic and much loved host on Love Island - we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success."Love Island is one of the most popular reality TV shows in the UK but the series has polarised viewers, with some arguing the show is misogynistic and raising concerns about the welfare of contestants.Ofcom has previously received tens of thousands of complaints about Love Island including about alleged misogynistic and bullying behaviour by some contestants.The watchdog has previously described the show as "emotionally charged" with "confrontational scenes" that can upset some viewers.Jama first built her profile through radio including a role on Rinse FM, before landing a presenting role on BBC Radio 1 in 2018.She went on to present a string of television programmes, including Channel 4's Stand Up To Cancer and ITV2's Don't Hate the Playaz, before taking over as host of BBC Three's Glow Up: Britain's Next Make-Up Star in 2021.The presenter was recently watched by millions in the Celebrity Traitors final, and competed as a traitor alongside actor Richard E Grant, Youtuber King Kenny and comedian James Acaster during the series.One commentator at the time said that, despite not winning the show, she had emerged as a winner of sorts as she was able to portray herself as "less like the presenter of Love Island and more like a genuinely versatile television star".Her Celebrity Traitors appearance came after she made her acting debut in the second series of Guy Ritchie's Netflix drama The Gentlemen alongside Theo James and Kaya Scodelario.Jama had auditioned for the cult Channel 4 series Skins, set in her hometown of Bristol, when she was 15, reaching the final stage for a role in the show that launched the careers of actors Daniel Kaluuya and Dev Patel.She moved to London when she was 16 to pursue a career in the entertainment industry.She began presenting a weekly music video countdown for production company JumpOff TV before joining MTV in 2014 as a presenter on The Wrap Up.Jama became the youngest person to host the MOBO Awards, alongside Marvin Humes, in 2017.

schema.headline: Maya Jama steps down as host of reality TV show Love Island

title: Sunderland 1-0 Chelsea: Xabi Alonso tinkers again as Blues lose to Black Cats
description: Constant changes in formation and personnel - and another disappointing defeat.Xabi Alonso's frustration was obvious as Chelsea's struggles for identi
body: Constant changes in formation and personnel - and another disappointing defeat.Xabi Alonso's frustration was obvious as Chelsea's struggles for identity continued in the 1-0 defeat by Sunderland.It is starting to feel as though the Spaniard is the latest "Tinkerman" at Stamford Bridge, a moniker first associated with Blues boss Claudio Ranieri back in 2002-03.For the first time this season, Chelsea lined up with a three-man midfield - but they were also without a recognised striker for the second match in a row, with Pedro Neto again struggling to lead the line in their loss at the Stadium of Light.By contrast, struggling Sunderland were led by target man Brian Brobbey, who won a 36th-minute penalty after being brought down by Levi Colwill. Enzo le Fee converted the game's only goal from the spot.That decision came moments after Chelsea were denied a penalty when Cole Palmer went down under a challenge from Luke O'Nien, but the video assistant referee ruled that contact had started outside the box.Those two incidents in quick succession meant Alonso and his coaching staff appeared angry on the touchline after the Sunderland goal.However, the Chelsea manager refused to criticise the officials after the game - instead he gave brief answers that changed the subject and were critical towards his players for not carrying out the gameplan properly.Asked whether Brobbey was simply unstoppable, Alonso, 44, replied: "No, he's stoppable. He's stoppable, but we have to do it better than we did today."Out of almost nothing he got a couple of chances. He got the penalty as well."I'm not happy with how we defended that situation. It's something that we could have avoided, something that we had worked on during the week. To concede penalties is not good for us."It left nowhere to hide for Colwill, who was substituted at half-time, with Moises Caicedo filling in at centre-back despite having barely completed a full training session all week and needing careful management of his own fitness issues.Chelsea also created few clear chances, aside from a headed opportunity that £117m signing Morgan Rogers squandered, while Palmer also struggled - days after being left out of the England squad.Before the season started, Alonso said he wanted his Chelsea side to be "unpredictable".Although factors such as injuries are beyond his control, his side have achieved that, but to their own detriment.Only Tottenham (28) have made more more line-up changes than Chelsea (24) in the Premier League this season.In the early part of the campaign, they at least had a settled and exciting front three of Joao Pedro, Rogers and Palmer. It was largely the reason behind the positive start to the season despite failing to keep a clean sheet against top-flight opposition until Alonso's eighth game in charge.With Caicedo injured, they suffered problems in midfield and continued to make changes from match to match, while also experimenting with personnel to fix the defence.However, they largely looked on course to emulate the back-three system Alonso excelled with during his historic German double-winning season at Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24.As Caicedo returned after the international break, however, captain Reece James was injured.Joao Pedro featured in wins against Bournemouth and Everton before sustaining a thigh injury, having already missed Brazil's international matches.Number one goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez broke his jaw in a collision at Everton, while Maxence Lacroix, who had been a near ever-present since joining from Crystal Palace in the summer, is expected to be out until January with a hamstring injury.Defender Jorrel Hato has also suffered a setback in recent weeks.It has left Alonso reacting to events when selecting his starting XI, with the Spaniard saying: "There are situations. Yesterday Josh [Acheampong] said he was not ready to play, so we are short of options and we need to walk through this step."Even when we win, when we lose, we miss some players that we have injured and for sure we are waiting for them to come back because they are important."He admitted his side were missing Joao Pedro, although supporters have also been frustrated that Estevao Willian, who came on at half-time on Sunday, has started only one league match this season.Prior to Sunday's game, Chelsea were averaging just 46% possession. They then dominated the ball at Sunderland (with 68.7% possession) but without creating many significant chances. Meanwhile, only Crystal Palace have conceded more shots on target than Chelsea's 50, while the Blues top the league with 53 shots on target - meaning there have been plenty of chances at both ends during their matches.Alonso can still be pleased with Chelsea having collected five more points than they managed from the equivalent fixtures last season, with the club on course to qualify for the Champions League while sitting fifth in the table.However, that is a low bar after a dismal campaign last season, when Chelsea finished 10th.Going into the November international break, Alonso remains a long way from establishing a style of play, or an identity capable of bringing consistency - although he promised promising in an interview last week that Chelsea would be "different" and "better" by the end of the season.

schema.headline: Sunderland 1-0 Chelsea: Xabi Alonso tinkers again as Blues lose to Black Cats

title: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row
description: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoin
body: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has rejected accusations of politicising Remembrance Sunday after being criticised for linking the event to the UK rejoining the European Union's Erasmus scheme.Her department announced on Saturday night that "as we mark Remembrance Sunday, Erasmus+ will give a new generation the chance to build connections across Europe".That sparked a backlash from the Conservatives, who said "veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme" and accused her of making an "EU membership pitch".Nandy said she was "horrified" by the Tory response and insisted that the expanded EU scheme for study and work would help young Britons recognise wartime sacrifice.The UK is rejoining the scheme in January, six years after leaving it as part of the Brexit deal.On Saturday, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport drew comparisons between that scheme and events on Sunday to commemorate veterans who had died in conflict.Referring to the scheme, Nandy said in her department's press release: "As we remember the immense courage of those who served our country, we honour them by building the best opportunities for the next generation through closeness and collaboration with our allies."Conservative Party chairman Kevin Hollinrake described her comments as "tone deaf and frankly shameful" and called on Nandy to apologise.He said the bonds that veterans forged "run far deeper" than Erasmus."It is not a day for a Labour minister to try to make an EU membership pitch," he added.Reform leader Nigel Farage told the BBC: "For Lisa Nandy to use Remembrance Sunday to announce this and say it's all about peace, it's all about the war - I find that very, very poor taste."Peter Sharples, chief executive of the Veterans Institute, told the Telegraph that people should "just honour the fallen" on Remembrance Sunday rather than discussing "party political matters".Asked about the criticism on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, Nandy stood by her initial remarks."It was Winston Churchill after the Second World War who talked about extending the hand of friendship across Europe and making sure that we honoured the legacy of that generation," she said.She said that after Brexit "we closed off opportunities for young people from this country to understand not just the impact that generation made here in the UK, but the way in which they went off and fought for the freedom of people across Europe".Asked to respond to accusations she had chosen Remembrance Sunday to "promote part of the new deal the government has done with the EU", Nandy said she was "not choosing today or any day actually to promote a deal with the EU".Pressed about linking the day to what the government believes are the cultural benefits of the scheme, Nandy said: "There was a time where that wouldn't have even raised an eyebrow as somehow political, it was just common sense - and it is common sense."The UK is paying £570m to join the expanded Erasmus+ scheme, external, which the government said was a 30% discount. It will include free year-abroad placements for UK university students and their European peers as well as cultural exchanges.The government said free train passes would be available for 18-year-olds to visit EU countries by themselves or with up to five friends.Youth groups will also get to do short exchanges in other countries, with a focus on areas of the country less engaged by Erasmus previously such as the north of England and Midlands, the government said.Applications will open for Erasmus+ later this month.Farage described Erasmus as a "terrible scheme" and "wildly expensive" compared to the Turing Scheme, which ministers introduced in 2021 as a post-Brexit alternative.He also criticised ongoing negotiations between the UK and the EU for a new youth mobility scheme ahead of a major summit on 20 November.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.But the EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes.Nandy said on Sunday that most of the benefits of Brexit promised in 2016 "have not been realised" and "there are trade-offs and choices to be made" on Britain's future relationship with the EU.

schema.headline: Nandy rejects claims of politicising Remembrance Sunday after Erasmus row

title: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says
description: Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.Lisa Nandy said
body: Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe". The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."It came after the Sunday Times reported, external that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules"."When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers"."While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included in the measures.A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".That means platforms that have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules having "scope creep".He said a restriction on messaging for under-16s "would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch", and urged the government to "ensure any new restrictions are proportionate and effective."The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.In recent weeks, attention has turned to how a social media ban would be enforced. Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.Rani Govender, head of online child safety at the NSPCC, said the "real question" going forward was how the government ensured age checks were effective."But effective age checks are only part of the solution," she added. "Tech companies must also be required to build child safety into every platform, device and AI tool, so children are protected from harmful and illegal content and only able to access age-appropriate services."

schema.headline: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says

title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that po
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency."There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. "But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."Image source, Getty ImagesShould Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decadesDemocrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination."Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nominationOther rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race."It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said."But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shiftFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

title: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph
description: Figure caption, The King led the Royal Family and political leaders in the Remembrance Service in LondonByRoyal correspondentReporting fromthe Cenotap
body: Figure caption, The King led the Royal Family and political leaders in the Remembrance Service in LondonByRoyal correspondentReporting fromthe Cenotaph, WhitehallKing Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath at the CenotaphImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Queen Camilla and Catherine, Princess of Wales, watched the event from the balcony of the Foreign and Commonwealth OfficeThe Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office. Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Veterans arrived at Whitehall ahead of the serviceThe poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.Image source, Press AssociationImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, "In everlasting remembrance" the King wrote on the wreath he laid at the CenotaphImage source, Press AssociationImage caption, Annie Duplock had joined the Land Army at the age of 16Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire."I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said."I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, (Top left to bottom right) former Prime Ministers Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson, Theresa May, Lord Cameron, Gordon Brown, Sir Tony Blair and Sir John MajorImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally led those gathered at the Cenotaph in prayerPrime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."Remembrance events took place across the country as thousands gathered to pay their respects to those who died in past conflicts.First Minister of Scotland John Swinney placed a wreath at the Stone of Remembrance outside the City Chambers during an event in Edinburgh.Veterans, military personnel and cadets also marched through the centres of British cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds.A silent poppy drop was held as part of the Festival of Remembrance at Durham Cathedral while wreaths were laid at Canterbury Cathedral.Separately, the Duke of Sussex was seen attending a Remembrance service in the market town of Brackley in Northamptonshire.Image source, Getty ImagesImage source, Getty ImagesFor more than a century, the national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect. Get in touchHave you taken part in a parade or service this weekend? Share your experience.

schema.headline: King leads solemn Remembrance Sunday service at Cenotaph

title: Top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries 'a hard yes' on impeaching Pete Hegseth
description: The top Democrat widely expected to be the next US House of Representatives Speaker has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete
body: The top Democrat widely expected to be the next US House of Representatives Speaker has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries told ABC's programme This Week that Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran".Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, a foe of President Donald Trump, has said he plans as early as Monday to introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth, which could result in his removal from office.The Pentagon told the BBC it had followed the law and that Hegseth would not be deterred by "phony investigations".As the current Democratic minority leader in the House, Jeffries is favourite to become Speaker when his party takes control of Congress in January following their landslide victory in last week's midterm elections. "I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC on Sunday."Pete Hegseth has got to go," he continued. Kentucky congressman Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, alleging that he made war on Iran without the required congressional authorisation under the War Powers Resolution of 1973.President Trump defended Hegseth on Sunday and pushed back againt Democrats' calls to impeach the Pentagon chief."They want to impeach him. Very unfair," Trump told CBS News' 60 Minutes. "We had two wars, we won both. We won Venezuela, we won Iran."Jeffries has vowed that the newly empowered Democrats will serve as a check and balance on the Trump administration. But he said after the midterms results that House Democrats were not currently focused on impeaching President Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term.Last week, Hegseth released a nearly six-minute video urging Congress to approve the Pentagon's latest military budget request, before the Republican-controlled legislature's final days come to an end. In the clip, he addressed talks of Massie's impeachment effort, referring to the threat as "sham articles". "You see, their policies don't work. So, their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents," Hegseth said. "It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me." Impeachment is a rare process by which the House of Representatives can vote to find an official guilty of misconduct and the Senate can then vote to remove the person from office.With more midterm races still to be called, Democrats have a 254-seat majority in the House, well beyond the 218 threshold needed to pass articles of impeachment.But they will fall well short of the two-thirds Senate majority required to remove an official from office, and would require Republicans to side with them - a politically high bar.

schema.headline: Top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries 'a hard yes' on impeaching Pete Hegseth

title: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
description: Action from "across society" is needed to help improve the educational outcomes of white working-class children, the co-chair of an independent inquir
body: Action from "across society" is needed to help improve the educational outcomes of white working-class children, the co-chair of an independent inquiry looking into the issue has said.The inquiry's first report, published this summer, concluded that once-in-a-generation reforms were needed to fix a system "not serving the interests of white working-class children".The next phase will focus on early years children and teenagers aged 14 to 19, aiming for a stronger start at primary school and improving older students' routes through education into successful careers.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "backing" the inquiry to "get to the heart of the barriers holding children back".Inquiry co-chair and former education secretary Baroness Morris said the next phase of the inquiry's work will consider "what needs to be done"."This isn't just the responsibility of schools but calls for action from across society," she said.The Independent Inquiry into White Working Class Educational Outcomes, external was commissioned by the multi-academy trust Star Academies, and is supported by the Department for Education.It spoke to thousands of young people and their parents, as well as hundreds of teachers.Education data about white working class pupils was also analysed as part of the year-long review, looking at the 1.25 million young people in England who are white British and in receipt of free school meals.The inquiry found a growing belief among white working-class families that the current education system does not guarantee future success.In the summer, the inquiry also acknowledged that the true scale of white working-class disadvantage is "likely to be substantially larger", as the education data they looked at did not include families who were on low incomes but did not receive free school meals.Since then, all families receiving Universal Credit have become eligible for free school meals.Under the new phase of the inquiry, practical recommendations for government, schools, colleges and other organisations working with white working-class communities will be developed.This action will include a research programme looking at the routes taken by teenagers aged 14 to 19, investigating how schools can work with communities to provide clearer pathways into further study and successful employment.The new phase of the inquiry will also look at how schools can ensure the transition from primary to secondary school builds strong foundations."Right now, too many white working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education," Powell said."That is why I am backing this independent inquiry to get to the heart of the barriers holding children back - from their first steps into school, through to the opportunities and choices they have as teenagers into further study, training or work."It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to open up new technical routes from age 14 in England over the summer.The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet".Currently, nearly a million young people are classed as Neet. Former minister Alan Milburn's interim report, external found that children who are not school-ready at aged four or five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet by ages 16 to 17.A final report by Milburn is expected to set out his recommendations for tackling the issue in the coming weeks.

schema.headline: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
